Title: This Is How You Lose the Time War
Author: Amal El-Mohtar
My Review:
First things first, I understand why so many people feel aggrieved by this book. It’s marketed as science fiction about time travel, war, and enemies to lovers, and technically, all of that is true. But it’s also misleading. This is, first and foremost, poetry. Once you understand that, the flowery prose and endless metaphors stop feeling like an affront to storytelling because it was never really about the story in the conventional sense.

Blue and Red, as we never learn their true names, are enigmas. They exist as paradoxes of tenderness and destruction. They are as capable of loving as they are of killing, and in their world, those acts are not contradictions but two expressions of the same devotion. Their relationship thrives on risk. They trust each other enough to risk betrayal, knowing that betraying the other would mean exposing their own compromise. They live on that knife edge, bound by shared peril, exhilarated by it. I believe at first it was their thrill-seeking, pain-loving nature that convinced them to exchange letters, but with time that changed. The craving for something tainted bled into a longing for something tangible and familiar in an existence where neither past nor future truly aligns.

Who cares that these two time travelling agents are at war? (Well, I care a little, but that’s beside the point.) What matters is that they are both intense and lonely, painfully aware of how out of place they are even among their own kind. Disjointed and different in a way that cannot be seen, only felt. Though their factions are opposites, they are mirrors. Each devours the world with the same hunger and finds in the other someone who can finally bear the weight of their existence. They are, at their core, the same.

Their letters form a tapestry of history, art, trauma, and solitude. They know each other through words alone, more intimately than most people know their lovers. At times the prose feels impenetrable, but that too feels right. Their correspondence is encrypted to everyone but its intended recipient, and we are merely eavesdropping. Their words are too alive, too private, too strange for us to fully understand. The language is lush and tangled because love in its truest form rarely translates cleanly. It must be felt through the static.

For me, this book, this anthology of letters, was something rare and beautiful. It is longing made language, passion distilled to ink, and it deserves every ounce of praise it receives.

Title: Assassin's Apprentice (Farseer Trilogy, #1)
Author: Robin Hobb
My Review:
Like a flower that blooms unseen, Fitz changed quietly between the folds of the pages. He became something so familiar it felt like a reflection. Not because we are alike, but because I came to know him so well that he felt like a part of myself.

Writing, at its best, is a kind of engineering. It is designing and crafting something so intricate that it remains in motion even when step away. Hobb does this with extraordinary precision.

Her characters feel alive, every detail moving with purpose. Fitz, our lonely and lovable protagonist, is shaped with reverence. He is gentle, capable, intelligent, and heartbreakingly alone. A boy born of love and shame, carrying both like a second skin.

What gives the story its pulse is the cast that surrounds him. Each is selfish and flawed, guiding Fitz as much as they wound him. Their quiet cruelties make his isolation almost unbearable. Through their tangled relationships, Hobb makes the world itself begin to breathe.

Fitz’s story is not grand or glorious. It is the story of what it means to remain good when goodness gains you nothing.

Yet the ending falters. The reflections fade, the rhythm breaks, and the boy who once felt so known slips through our fingers. I imagine Hobb meant to mirror Fitz’s confusion but the execution feels rushed. The clarity that once defined him is lost, leaving Fitz’s logic unclear. At times he acted so unlike himself that I no longer recognised the boy I had come to know.

Even so, the book remains remarkable. The ending cost it perfection, but not beauty.

4.5 stars.

Title: Children of Time (Children of Time, #1)
Author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
My Review:
Children of Time felt like a love letter to Darwin’s theory of evolution, a sweeping dream about progress and adaptation, tied into a book that often read more like a thesis than a novel.

Tchaikovsky brilliantly highlights that what makes humanity great is also what makes it terrible. Our strengths are our flaws; what builds us also breaks us. The intrigue lies not in the cycle, but in how we attempt to break it.

The book shines in its depiction of civilisation rising and falling. The events unfold with such cohesion and inevitability that it reads less like invention and more like a historical record. The concept is executed with incredible scope and intelligence and an almost clinical precision.

But that is also why it did not surpass four stars for me. Children of Time failed to fully engage me on an emotional level.

We follow the spiders’ accelerated evolution in snapshots across centuries. It is a fascinating narrative device, but it means we never stay with a single character long enough to form a true attachment. Instead of individual arcs, we witness the development of a species. While this is clever, it leaves the spiders, despite their mimicry of human society with religion and fanaticism, feeling more like case studies than characters.

The humans aboard the Gilgamesh provide the emotional counterpoint, but even here the execution fell flat. The narrative often revisits the same handful of crew members, yet they lack weight as protagonists. Holsten, the supposed central perspective, feels more like a passive observer than an active participant. Lain shows far more spark and depth, but we are rarely given the chance to see the story through her eyes.

The result is a book that is impressive, expansive, and deeply intelligent, but not immersive. At times, it felt like I was reading a study on a fascinating subject: intellectually gratifying, yes, but often heavy, even homework like.

For that reason, I will not be continuing the series. Still, I cannot fault Tchaikovsky’s vision or skill, and I would recommend Children of Time to readers with a scientific or historical inclination. It is a remarkable piece of speculative fiction, just not one that left me emotionally invested.
